persona.goal: Go from zero ML knowledge to training and evaluating a small image classifier in PyTorch

user_context.background: Mechanical engineer moving into ML; comfortable with Python scripting, numpy and linear algebra from university
user_context.constraints: I learn best from code-along videos but I want to understand the math intuition too. Long courses are fine. I can only study 90 minutes at a sitting, so split long courses into parts.

expectations.notes: Huge budget: should use most of 20 hours with a prerequisite chain (ML basics -> gradients -> tensors/autograd -> training loop -> CNN -> evaluation); long courses legitimate.

plan.interpretation: The learner can explain core ML and backpropagation intuition, then write and run a PyTorch training loop for a small CNN image classifier and evaluate it for overfitting and accuracy.
assumptions: The 1200 minutes is pure viewing time, so it covers about 20 hours of videos with no time reserved for practice.
Because the learner likes code-along videos, the plan favors tutorials where the presenter writes code live.
'Small image classifier' means a CNN trained on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST or CIFAR-10, not a large pretrained model pipeline.
Each video or course part should fit within a 90-minute sitting, so long courses are picked in chunks of 90 minutes or less.
Calculus and linear algebra are already known, so math-focused videos should build intuition for ML and not reteach prerequisites.

sub_topics.title: Machine learning fundamentals: models, loss, features, train/test split
sub_topics.why: The learner has no ML background, so they need the vocabulary and framing (supervised learning, loss functions, generalization) before touching neural networks.

sub_topics.title: Gradient descent and backpropagation intuition and math
sub_topics.why: The learner knows calculus, so they can learn the chain rule applied to computation graphs and see how weights are updated, which gives the math intuition they want.

sub_topics.title: PyTorch tensors and autograd
sub_topics.why: The learner knows numpy, so tensors map to familiar ideas. They need to learn the PyTorch API, GPU/device handling, and how autograd computes gradients.

sub_topics.title: Building neural networks and training loops in PyTorch
sub_topics.why: They need to write nn.Module models, pick loss functions and optimizers, use DataLoaders and run the train/eval loop end to end.

sub_topics.title: Convolutional neural networks: convolutions, pooling, architectures
sub_topics.why: Image classification needs CNNs. A linear algebra background helps with understanding convolution as a sliding dot product and with feature maps and shapes.

sub_topics.title: Model evaluation, overfitting, and regularization
sub_topics.why: The learner must measure accuracy and tell whether the model generalizes, using validation splits, loss curves, confusion matrices, data augmentation, dropout and weight decay.

sub_topics.title: Build and train an image classifier end to end in PyTorch
sub_topics.why: A code-along project ties everything together: load an image dataset, build a CNN, train it, evaluate it, and iterate to improve results.

warnings: Under-filled: only about 324 of 1200 minutes are used (~27%), roughly 876 unused. The pool has no long courses and few substantial PyTorch tutorials, and I did not pad with weak or redundant videos.
None of the cards has verified quotes, so evidence_quote_ids is empty for every pick. Reasons rest on the card summaries and metadata, and confidence is moderated for that.

Thin coverage of PyTorch tensors and autograd: the only usable pick is the StatQuest intro, which is flagged surface_intro. Consider supplementing with the official PyTorch tutorials or a longer PyTorch course.
Evaluation coverage is mostly conceptual (bias/variance, regularization). No video clearly shows a train/validation/test split or tracking accuracy in code, so do this yourself in the project.
Sittings: all picks fit within 90 minutes. The 78-minute CS229 lecture should be its own sitting; group the shorter videos into sessions of at most 90 minutes.

Several picks (codebasics CNN explainer, TensorFlow-based) use different tooling for concepts; transfer to PyTorch is assumed. Upload dates of 2026 on a few cards look odd but there is no date floor, so I ignored them.
Practice time is not included in the budget; consider coding along with the videos and reproducing the CIFAR-10 project yourself.
